## Paper

## Abstract

Aqueous Zn metal batteries offer a safe, low-cost route to grid-scale energy storage yet suffer from dendrite growth and corrosion issues. Conventional electrolyte designs largely overlook electric-field-driven interfacial dynamics such as solvation structure evolution and component redistribution during operation. Here, we propose an affinitive additive strategy featuring high donor number and dipole moment, exemplified by N,N-dimethylurea (DMU), to dynamically modulate Zn2+ solvation and the structure of the electric double layer under operational electric fields. Guided by physically grounded molecular descriptors, we identify additives capable of electric-field-induced interfacial enrichment, during which strong dipole-field coupling promotes their incorporation into the Zn2+ solvation shell and promotes more uniform Zn deposition. As a result, the optimized electrolyte achieves a coulombic efficiency of ~99.9% for Zn plating/stripping with only 2 wt% additive. It also sustains stable operation for 700 h at 60% depth of discharge, outperforming the baseline electrolyte. Descriptor-guided screening further reveals that other candidates follow the same pattern, suggesting broader applicability of this approach. Practical Zn||ZnI2 full cells with high areal capacity (~3 mAh cm-2) and low N/P ratio (~1.8) achieve 750 stable cycles at 0.15 A g-1 with 84.5% capacity retention.

---

## Introduction

Aqueous batteries, with their intrinsic safety, low cost, and environmental compatibility, have emerged as viable alternatives for large-scale electrical energy storage1–3. In particular, Zn metal batteries (ZMBs) combine low redox potential, high theoretical capacity, and the use of abundant raw materials, making them attractive candidates for grid-scale storage4. Nevertheless, the thermodynamic instability of Zn in aqueous electrolytes promotes persistent parasitic hydrogen evolution reactions (HER) and corrosion during plating/stripping cycles. As a result, these irreversible side reactions degrade coulombic efficiency (CE) and severely undermine the cycle life essential for practical applications5,6. Besides, Zn negative electrodes also suffer from dendritic growth, a common issue with metal negative electrodes. Consequently, addressing the fundamental negative-electrode-related challenges in ZMBs remains a critical hurdle for commercialization.

Electrolyte engineering has emerged as a powerful strategy for mitigating the interfacial irreversibility of Zn metal negative electrodes7–9, particularly in aqueous systems where dendrite growth, hydrogen evolution, and parasitic corrosion are prevalent. By modulating Zn2+ coordination environments and interfacial ion distributions, solvation structure tailoring10–14 and electric double layer (EDL) engineering15,16 have enabled notable improvements in reversibility and cycling stability. However, these advances remain constrained by inherent trade-offs. Dilute electrolytes offer insufficient interfacial regulation due to excessive water activity, while highly concentrated systems introduce challenges including elevated viscosity, sluggish ion transport, and increased cost17,18. In parallel, many formulations rely on high loadings of organic co-solvents (>10 wt%)19, which compromise safety margins and scale-up viability. These limitations reflect a broader conceptual gap: most existing strategies assume static solvation and interfacial behavior and depend on empirical additive screening without accounting for the dynamic electric field environment that governs real-time interfacial processes during operation. A critical yet often overlooked factor underlying these limitations is the dynamic nature of the electrode-electrolyte interface. In practical operation, intense interfacial electric fields, ranging from 105 to 107 V cm-120,21, continuously modulate the spatial distribution of ions and solvent molecules, dynamically reshaping Zn2+ solvation shells and interfacial composition. These field-driven perturbations profoundly impact nucleation behavior, surface reactivity, and additive functionality, yet remain largely unaddressed in conventional electrolyte design. Incorporating this dynamic perspective could provide a foundation for rational additive selection, particularly for systems engineered to respond to operational electric fields in situ.

In this work, we report an affinitive additive design for improved reversibility in aqueous ZMBs. Specifically, these affinitive additives combine high donor number (DN) and dipole moment (μ), enabling dual functionality: high‑DN molecules engage in stronger coordination interactions with Zn2+, while high-μ imparts strong electric-field-responsiveness. Unlike prior cosolvent engineering strategies, our framework explicitly treats the electrode’s interfacial electric field as an active driver of additive migration and adsorption, rather than a passive environment. A combination of experimental and computational methods revealed that under operational polarization, these additives dynamically redistribute to the electric double layer, modulating Zn2+ solvation environments. We further establish DN and μ as practical molecular-level descriptors that predict field-responsive enrichment, providing a generalizable selection rule. Building on this descriptor framework, we performed a high-throughput computational-experimental screening to identify additional molecules that satisfy DN-μ criterion, further supporting the broader applicability of this design approach. When incorporated into a ZnSO4 electrolyte (BE), this electric-field-reinforced affinitive electrolyte (ERAE) exhibits rapid interfacial accumulation of additives, modulating the Zn2+ solvation shell and markedly extending negative electrode lifespan. ERAE(DMU) achieves a Zn plating/stripping CE of 99.9% and demonstrates high compatibility with diverse positive electrode materials such as V6O13 and ZnI2, enabling stable full-cell cycling at high mass loadings.

---

## Results

Design principles of additives
Achieving effective interfacial regulation at low additive concentrations relies on a clear mechanistic understanding of Zn2+ solvation and its interplay with interfacial electric fields. To this end, we begin by examining how Zn2+ interacts with its surrounding environment, as the solvation structure strongly influences ion transport and deposition behavior13. In aqueous ZMBs, Zn2+ functions as a Lewis acid that coordinates with solvent molecules or additives containing lone-pair electrons. Molecules with high DN donate electron density more efficiently to Zn2+,22,23 forming stable coordination complexes that enable co-migration under an applied electric field24,25. Meanwhile, species with larger μ exhibit strong dipole-field interactions, allowing them to align under electric fields and lower interfacial free energy, which enhances their adsorption26. Guided by this dual-parameter principle, we constructed a molecular library spanning a wide range of DN and μ values, and evaluated each candidate’s interfacial behavior under realistic field conditions. As shown in Figure 1a, we identified three types of additive response: electric-field-weakened shielding electrolytes (EWSE) with low μ cannot compete with water for interfacial adsorption; electric-field-weakened inert electrolytes (EWIE) with low DN lack coordination ability and fail to migrate; ERAE with both high DN and μ tend to exhibit strong co‑migration and sustained interfacial retention.

To systematically assess the effectiveness of additive-induced interfacial regulation, we screened 12 additives spanning a broad range of DN, μ, the adiabatic ionization energies (AIEs) and adiabatic electron affinities (AEAs), each introduced at a fixed loading of 2 wt% (Figures S1, S2 and Table S1). Electrochemical Zn plating/stripping tests were conducted using Zn‖Zn symmetric cells under harsh conditions (60 μL electrolyte, 60% depth of discharge (DOD); Figure S3), which ensured that observed performance differences could be primarily attributed to interfacial effects. We found that Zn plating/stripping duration correlated strongly and reproducibly with the combined DN-μ descriptor, supporting the predictive value of our design approach (Figures S4-S6). Interestingly, neither DN nor μ alone showed clear correlation with stability, nor did other common properties (Figure S7). This observation reinforces the importance of jointly considering both DN and μ when selecting affinitive additives. We further refined our analysis by employing a machine learning approach to identify the optimal feature pair (Figure 1b and Table S2). Twelve features, including dipole moment, dielectric constant, donor number, ET, and total polar surface area, were selected to generate 66 unique feature pairs. Utilizing Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) with Ridge regression, we assessed each pair’s performance. The DN-μ combination yielded the lowest root mean square error, identifying it as a robust descriptor pair for predicting additive efficacy.

As shown in Figure 1c, the Zn plating/stripping duration achieved at 60 % DOD is plotted against each additive’s DN and μ, with bubble size representing performance. Additives located in the upper-right quadrant, combining both high DN and high μ, generally achieved lifetimes exceeding 200 hours, reflecting strong interfacial enrichment and stabilization even at low concentration. In contrast, additives with low μ are displaced by water at the interface, while those with low DN lacked the coordination ability needed for co-migration with Zn2+. As a result, neither class improved negative electrode lifetime relative to the BE, and in several cases, even reduced it. Conversely, ERAE showed clear improvements in Zn plating/stripping duration. This overall trend, mapped against molecular descriptors, highlights the utility of the DN-μ design framework. Based on these results, ERAE(DMU) and ERAE(MF) emerged as the potential candidates (Figure S8), both extending the Zn plating/stripping duration (Figure S5). Among them, DMU was selected as the principal focus for subsequent studies because it combines strong electrochemical performance with practical advantages in terms of safety and sustainability.

Electric-field-induced EDL reconfiguration
To gain deeper insights into the reconfiguration of the electric double layer (EDL) under applied electric fields, we conducted a comprehensive analysis using in situ electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (eQCM) coupled with cyclic voltammetry (CV). This technique enables real-time monitoring of additive adsorption and desorption dynamics at the electrode-electrolyte interface27. Three different types of electrolytes were evaluated in 2 m ZnSO4. Electrode mass changes were detected via quartz-crystal frequency shifts following the Sauerbrey relation28. When paired with CV, this setup enables continuous tracking of interfacial mass variations29. Importantly, additives in the ERAE region undergo clear field-driven adsorption/desorption (Figure 2a), as revealed by the combined Pearson-amplitude ratio (AR) analysis in Figures 2b, S9. The Pearson coefficient captures the directional consistency between potential and mass variation, while the AR, extracted from the fundamental oscillation of the mass response, quantifies the strength of electric-field-induced adsorption/desorption. ERAE additives show large negative Pearson values together with high AR, consistent with strong electro-responsiveness. By contrast, EWIE, EWSE, and BE additives exhibit weak correlation and minimal AR values, indicating negligible mass modulation under the applied field. Control QCM measurements on Zn-coated QCM sensors suggest that the observed mass changes are not due to specific chemical adsorption (Figures S10-S12). Based on these observations, we infer that high-DN, high-μ additives accumulate at the Zn surface under field, leading to the formation of an organic-rich EDL. This is evidenced by a pronounced decrease in electric double‑layer capacitance (EDLC) and Mott-Schottky analysis (Figures S13, S14), which reflects the field-driven enrichment of additives. This conclusion is further supported by the reduced Arrhenius activation energy under an applied electric field (Figure S46) To assess the protective effect of this organic‑rich EDL, differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) was used to monitor H2 evolution during cycling. Results show that the BE produces consistently higher H2 levels with intermittent bubble-detachment spikes19. In contrast, the ERAE(DMU) substantially reduces gas evolution (Figure 2c). Because the HER is strongly suppressed in ERAE(DMU), fewer byproducts are generated, as confirmed by XRD (Figure S15), and the interfacial passivation layer is correspondingly much thinner, as revealed by XPS depth profiling (Figure S16) and TEM imaging (Figure S17). These results suggest that affinitive additives enrich the EDL and suppress parasitic H2 evolution.

To further elucidate the electric-field-induced reconfiguration of the EDL at the Zn electrode interface, we performed constant-potential molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with and without applied bias (Figures 2d, 2e and S18-S20). When an external electric field is applied, DMU molecules accumulate strongly at the interface, demonstrating clear field responsiveness. By contrast, EWIE(SL) shows no field-induced enhancement, with its interfacial distribution remaining nearly unchanged under bias. Quantitative analysis (Figure 2f) further reveals that the surface coverage of ERAE increases markedly under bias, positioning them above the diagonal line, while EWSE and EWIE lie below the line, reflecting their depleted interfacial populations. This field-responsive enrichment suggests that affinitive additives can dynamically reorganize the interfacial environment under electric field, which is associated with reduced parasitic reactions and improved Zn negative electrode stability.

Interfacial dynamics of Zn2+ solvation shells
The interfacial dynamics of Zn2+ solvation are also important for efficient additive design. To further elucidate the dynamic modulation of the Zn2+ solvation shells by ERAE(DMU) under operational electric fields, in situ attenuated-total-reflectance Fourier-transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy was conducted in combination with chronoamperometry to record the time evolution of absolute absorbance, [A(t)] (Figures S21, S22). In addition, surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAS) was employed to selectively probe interfacial species with higher sensitivity (Figures S23, S24), thereby complementing the ATR-FTIR analysis. This technique enables real-time monitoring of interfacial chemical environments, providing insights into solvation dynamics during Zn plating and stripping processes30. Relative absorbance changes, [A(t)-A(t0)], were calculated by subtracting the initial spectrum recorded at t0. We then analyzed [A(t)-A(t0)] over the plating (t0-t900) and stripping (t900-t1800) intervals. Notably, the relative absorbance variations closely track the current response, particularly for the O-H stretching vibration [ν(H2O)] and asymmetric S-O stretching [ν(SO42-)]. The ν(H2O) includes contributions from both weak (W-H) and strong (S-H) hydrogen bonds. Consistent with previous studies31, in the BE, ν(SO42-) absorbance decreases during plating, indicating that SO42- moves away from the interface. During stripping, ν(SO42-) absorbance increases, suggesting that SO42- returns toward the interface. Additionally, hydrogen bonding (HB) in water weakens during plating and strengthens during stripping (Figure 3a). In stark contrast, in the ERAE(DMU), changes in ν(H2O) and ν(SO42-) are markedly suppressed (Figure 3b). SEIRAS demonstrates that ERAE(DMU) undergoes potential-dependent dynamic adsorption and desorption and adsorption at the electrode surface. This finding indicates that the variations of SO42- and H2O observed by in situ ATR-FTIR are instead induced by the interfacial adsorption of ERAE(DMU), highlighting its role in regulating the interfacial environment. These findings suggest that affinitive additives partially exclude both H2O and SO42- from the Zn2+ solvation shell at the interface. These observations are schematically illustrated in Figure 3c, where the dynamic reorganization of Zn2+ solvation shells under an applied field is depicted.

Subsequently, the interfacial Zn2+ hydration in ERAE(DMU) and BE was quantified in real time using in situ eQCM during the negative polarization process with carbon black-coated quartz crystals, which allows solvated Zn species to diffuse into the pore structure (Figure S25). The measured Δm-ΔQ relations were compared with the dotted and dashed theoretical mass, charge slopes corresponding to bare Zn2+ and fully hydrated Zn2+·6H2O, respectively. In the BE electrolyte, the Δm-ΔQ plot closely follows the theoretical behavior of the fully hydrated species, and the fitted slope corresponds to an apparent molar mass of 179 g mol-1 (details of the slope calculation and molar-mass extraction are provided in the Supporting Information). In contrast, the ERAE(DMU) electrolyte exhibits markedly larger mass changes per unit charge, yielding an apparent molar mass of 202 g mol-1. These heavier, less-hydrated interfacial Zn complexes suggest that the associative additive may participate in modifying the interfacial solvation environment by partially displacing water molecules from the primary solvation shell of Zn2+.

To quantitatively assess the electric-field-responsiveness of molecules in relation to their coordination with Zn2+, the binding energy (Eb) between each additive and Zn2+ was calculated as a measure of coordination strength. Electric-field-responsiveness was then evaluated for a series of molecules (Figure 3g). A strong positive correlation between Eb and field-responsiveness is observed for ERAE(DMAC, DMSO, DMU, DMF, NMP) indicating both high Zn2+ affinity and pronounced field sensitivity. By contrast, EWSE(MeOH), EWIE(ACN) and H2O exhibit weak Zn2+ binding and low field-responsiveness, indicating limited interfacial affinity. As the field strength increases from 0 to 0.2 ×10-3 V Å-1, Eb decreases markedly for EWIE(ACN), H2O, and EWSE(MeOH) (Figure S26). Among them, H2O shows the steepest decline, indicating facile stripping of water ligands under field. In contrast, ERAE(DMAC, DMU, DMF, NMP) exhibit slight increases in Eb, indicating their resistance to field-induced dissociation and further reinforcement of Zn2+ coordination. This behavior is consistent with field-driven enrichment and stabilization of Zn2+ solvation at the interface.

Furthermore, MD simulations were conducted to compare Zn2+ solvation structures under field-free (bulk) and applied-field (interfacial) conditions (Figure 3h). In the absence of bias, Zn2+ solvation is dominated by water molecules, and most additives show negligible participation in the primary solvation shell. Under an applied field, however, ERAE(DMAC, DMF, DMU, DMSO, NMP) partially replace water ligands and become incorporated into the Zn2+ solvation shell, reflecting their strong electric-field responsiveness. By contrast, EWIE (ACN, SL) and EWSE (TAA, TBA) remain largely excluded, indicating little contribution to field-driven solvation restructuring. These results highlight a dual-parameter design principle: additives that combine high Zn2+ binding affinity with strong dipolar response are more likely to accumulate at the interface and actively reorganize Zn2+ solvation under operating conditions.

To rule out bulk effects, ex situ ATR-FTIR, X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) and ionic conductivity measurements were performed on both BE and ERAE(DMU). These techniques probe coordination environment, local structure, and transport properties, respectively. ATR-FTIR spectra for BE and ERAE(DMU) (Figure S27) indicates similar Zn2+ coordination environments. Similarly, XANES data (Figure S28) show that the Zn K-edge absorption energies are virtually the same for BE and ERAE(DMU). FT-EXAFS fitting in R space confirms that the first-shell Zn-O coordination is preserved (Figure S29). Wavelet transform analyses (Figures S30, S31) likewise indicate that the local solvation sheath experiences only minimal perturbation. Together, these results indicate that at 2 wt% additive loading, ERAE(DMU) does not substantially infiltrate bulk Zn2+ solvation clusters despite their high DN. Moreover, BE and ERAE(DMU) display comparable ionic conductivities (Figure S32), confirming that bulk transport properties remain effectively constant. Therefore, the performance enhancements arise predominantly from interfacial, rather than bulk, additive effects.

Morphology of deposited Zn
Generally, interfacial Zn2+ solvation structure plays an important role in governing nucleation behavior32, so we next investigated its impact on deposition uniformity. Since electric‑field inhomogeneity at the metal-electrolyte interface is known to drive dendritic growth33, scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) was employed to map the local electric-field distributions across Zn deposit (Figure 4a). Ferrocene methanol (FcMeOH) served as a redox mediator, and its tip current was monitored to report field strength. SECM imaging revealed highly uniform current signals in the ERAE(DMU) (Figure 4b), whereas the BE exhibited distinct inhomogeneity with a depressed region in the center (Figure 4c). This field distortion is associated with uneven Zn2+ flux, which may promote preferential growth at the electrode edges and symmetry breaking in the nucleation pattern34. To observe the dynamic evolution of Zn plating, in situ optical microscopy was performed. The BE system showed increasing surface roughness and visible gas evolution over time, while the ERAE(DMU) exhibited a more compact and uniform deposition front (Figure 4d). Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) further confirmed these trends, with the BE showing a rougher and more disordered surface compared to the smoother morphology under the ERAE(DMU) (Figure 4e). High-resolution SEM images revealed dense, layered Zn deposits in the ERAE(DMU), in contrast to the porous and irregular structure observed in the BE (Figure 4f). Given that the electro-crystallization rate depends on overpotential and is reflected in current transients, potentiostatic experiments were performed. These measurements were used to probe Zn nucleation and growth kinetics. The resulting i-t curves (Figure S33) were normalized using the peak current (im) and corresponding time (tm), and compared with two classical models: the Scharifker-Hills (SH) model35 describing 3D diffusion-controlled hemispherical growth (3DI, 3DP), and the Bewick-Fleischmann-Thirsk (BFT) model36 describing 2D lateral cylindrical growth (2DI, 2DP) (Figure 4g). In the BE, Zn nucleation follows a mixed 2D/3D growth mode. Consequently, 3D growth produces rough, porous deposits that disrupt the uniformity of the Zn plating layer37. By contrast, in the ERAE(DMU), Zn deposition is consistent with a predominantly 2DP mode, leading to a smoother, homogeneous layer without pronounced agglomeration.

Electrochemical performance
Building on the observed interfacial behavior, the electrochemical performance of half cells was further evaluated. The Zn plating/stripping stability of Zn||Zn symmetric cells was assessed at DOD of 30%, 60%, 70%, and 80% using the ERAE(DMU). At 30 % DOD, ERAE(DMU) exhibited a Zn plating/stripping duration of 1625 h; at 60 % DOD, Zn plating/stripping duration was 700 h; at 70 % DOD, 455 h; and at 80 % DOD, 315 h (BE < 100h) (Figure 5a). Furthermore, under a stepwise high-DOD protocol (30%, 60%, 80%, 60%, 30%), the ERAE(DMU) maintained prolonged Zn plating/stripping stability (Figure 5b). Using Aurbach’s protocol38,39 at 60% DOD, Zn CE reached 99.92% in the ERAE(DMU) versus 97.82% in the BE (Figures 5c). CE measurements across all electrolytes (Figures S34-S37) show that ERAE consistently maintains the higher Coulombic efficiency during long-term cycling, indicating enhanced reversibility of Zn plating/stripping behavior. In contrast, EWIE and EWSE display lower reversibility and shorter lifetimes. These results suggest that affinitive additives enhance both Zn negative electrode stability and reversibility, with the improved performance arising from interfacial enrichment that modulates Zn2+ solvation clusters and promotes a water-deficient EDL. Considering DOD, cumulative plating capacity (CPC), and electrolyte cost, the Zn negative electrode metrics reported here achieve competitive performance (Figure 5d).

Furthermore, positive electrodes compatibility and full-cell performance under harsh conditions were explored. Zn||V6O13 (intercalation-type) full cells were assembled using the ERAE(DMU) to evaluate long-term stability and reversibility. The galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) profiles of the ERAE-based Zn||V6O13 cell at 0.3 A g-1 (Figure S38) closely match the characteristic V6O13 GCD profiles40. The N/P ratio was set to approximately 3. After 900 cycles, the ERAE-based Zn||V6O13 cell retained 87.5% capacity, with an average CE of 98.8% (Figure 6a). In comparison, the BE-based cell retained only 55% of capacity after just 200 cycles and then gradually faded to near zero, without short circuiting. This indicates that parasitic side reactions41, rather than dendrite‑induced failure, are the dominant cause of capacity loss. These findings suggest that ERAE(DMU) effectively suppresses parasitic reactions and improved Zn negative electrode durability in full cells.

Moreover, Zn||ZnI2 (conversion-type) full cells were also assembled under high mass loading conditions. GCD profiles at 1 C (0.15 A g-1) and 4 C exhibit typical ZnI2 positive electrode characteristics (Figure S39). Under harsh conditions (E/C ~ 16 µL mAh-1, N/P ~ 1.8), the ERAE(DMU) completed 750 cycles at 1 C, retaining 84.5% capacity with an average CE of 99% (Figure 6b). At 4 C rate, the cell sustained 1,000 cycles with 91.5% retention, indicating stable cycling performance and high-rate capability (Figure S40), as well as improved CE. In contrast, the BE showed large CE fluctuations and experienced short circuiting after 130 cycles. This failure is attributed to polyiodide shuttling, which accelerates parasitic reactions at the Zn negative electrode42 and leads to rapid Zn depletion and dendritic formation. Open-circuit voltage decay tests of fully charged Zn||ZnI2 cells after 24 h storage show 92.9% capacity retention in the ERAE(DMU), indicating effective suppression of polyiodide shuttling (Figure S41). The ERAE(DMU) also delivers high cumulative discharge capacity (CDC) at low electrolyte cost (Table S6). These results highlight the ability of ERAE(DMU) to stabilize Zn negative electrodes and enable durable, high-performance operation with conversion-type positive electrodes. To assess scale‑up feasibility, a Zn||ZnI2 pouch cell was fabricated using ERAE a 30 mg cm-2 ZnI2 positive electrode, a separator, and a 20 µm Zn negative electrode. This configuration yielded an areal capacity of 4 mAh cm-2, with an N/P ratio of approximately 3, and a total discharge capacity of 100 mAh for the 25 cm2 pouch cell. The cell exhibited stable polarization throughout cycling, with only a slight increase compared to the coin cell (Figure 6c). As a result, a long-term cycling stability of 200 cycles with 99.2% capacity retention was achieved (Figure 6d). Even when paired with MnO2 positive electrodes, ERAE(DMU) still exhibits enhanced cycling stability and higher CE compared with the BE, demonstrating its broad compatibility with different cathode chemistries (Figures S44, S45). Overall, the electric-field responsiveness of ERAE(DMU) enables stable and efficient cycling performance under demanding full-cell conditions.

High-throughput screening workflow
To explore the applicability of the DN-μ design principle beyond the additives experimentally examined in this work, we further developed a high-throughput computational screening pipeline (Figure 7a). Beginning with ~569,000 organic molecules downloaded from PubChem, we applied a sequence of filters based on toxicity, chemical stability, and pH compatibility, narrowing the pool to ~223,000 candidates. Additional constraints related to synthetic accessibility and commercial availability reduced this set to ~20,000 molecules. Efficient xTB calculations were then performed to evaluate three molecular-level criteria informed by our mechanistic understanding: (1) electrochemical stability (AIE > 10.4 eV and AEA < 6.4 eV), (2) high dipole moment (> 5.0 D), and (3) strong Zn-ion binding affinity (0.18 Hartree higher than Zn2+-H2O interaction).

Application of these criteria yielded ~300 promising candidates (Supplementary Data 1), which were subsequently filtered by cost and commercial accessibility, arriving at ~30 final molecules with DN-μ characteristics aligned with our design framework. To experimentally interrogate the predictive power of this screening strategy, we selected two inexpensive and commercially accessible additives (piracetam (PIR) and 1-(2-Hydroxyethyl)-2-pyrrolidone (HEP)) from this set and incorporated them into Zn||Zn symmetric cells. As shown in Figure 7b, both additives led to extended Zn plating/stripping duration: ERAE(HEP) achieved a lifetime of 270 h at 60% DOD, while the ERAE(PIR) achieved 615 h under the same conditions. These results provide experimental support for the applicability of our computational design logic.

## Methods

Chemical reagents
N,N-Dimethylurea (DMU, 98% purity), tert-Butanol (TBA, ≥ 99% purity), tert-Amyl alcohol (TAA, 99% purity), Methanol (MeOH, 99.5% purity), 1-Methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP, > 99.5% purity), N,N-Dimethylacetamide (DMAC, 99% purity), N-Methylformamide (MF, 99% purity), Triethyl phosphate (TEP, > 99.5% purity), Piracetam (PIR, > 98% purity), 1-(2-Hydroxyethyl)-2-pyrrolidone (HEP, > 99.5%), Ferrocene methanol (FcMeOH, 98% purity) and vanadium pentoxide (V2O5, 99% purity) were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Technology Co. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, > 99.8% purity), N,N-Dimethylformamide (DMF, > 99.9% purity) and Sulfolane (SL, 99% purity), Ethylene glycol (EG, > 99.5% purity) were purchased from Energy Chemical Co. Zinc sulfate heptahydrate (ZnSO4·7H2O) was purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Trimethyl phosphate (TMP, 98% purity), Zinc Iodide (ZnI2, 99% purity) were purchased from Shanghai Adamas Reagent Co, the gold plating solution was purchased from Shanghai Yuanfang Technology Co., Ltd, The commercial nanoscale α-MnO2 was purchased from Shanghai Yunfu Nano Technology Co., Ltd. Acetylene black (Kappa 100), CNT-3213, PTFE aqueous dispersion (60 wt%), Ketjen black (EC-600JD) and PVDF 5130 were purchased from Guangdong Canrd New Technology Co.

Electrolyte preparation
Deionized water was used as the solvent to prepare the aqueous electrolytes. BE (2m ZnSO4) was prepared by dissolving 0.02 mol ZnSO4·7H2O in 7.48g of H2O. The 2 wt% additive content was calculated based on the total mass of the mixed electrolyte.

Electrode preparation and cell assembly
V6O13 was prepared as follows43 (Figure S42, S43). Briefly, 0.9 g of vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) was dissolved in a mixture of 10 mL of ethanol and 30 mL of DI. After continuously stirring for 1 h, the solution was transferred to a 50 mL Teflon autoclave and heated at 180°C for 12 h. It was then washed several times with ethanol and dried overnight at 60°C in a vacuum atmosphere to obtain V6O13. For V6O13 free standing positive electrodes, a mixture of active material V6O13, acetylene black, CNTs and PTFE binder were pressed in a weight ratio of 7:1:1:1. For ZnI2 free standing positive electrodes, a mixture of active material ZnI2, activated carbon (YEC-8A, Fuzhou Yihuan Carbon Co., Ltd.), and PTFE binder was pressed in a weight ratio of 6:3:1. For α-MnO2 positive electrodes, a slurry was prepared by mixing α-MnO2, Ketjen black, and PVDF binder in a weight ratio of 7:2:1. The slurry was uniformly coated onto 39BB carbon paper (Toray) using a doctor blade, followed by drying overnight at 80 °C. Electrodes were cut into circular disks using a precision puncher. CR2032 coin cells (Guangdong Canrd New Technology Co.) were assembled for electrochemical measurements, maintained at 25°C in a temperature-controlled chamber (Shenzhen Neware Technology Co.). Zn||Cu cells were assembled by using Zn foil (thickness: 200 μm, diameter: 14 mm) as negative electrode and Cu foil (thickness: 20 μm, diameter: 19 mm) as positive electrode. Symmetrical cells were assembled by using two Zn foils (thickness: 10 μm, diameter: 12 mm). Full cells, including Zn||ZnI2, Zn||V6O13 were assembled by using thin Zn foil (thickness: 10 μm, diameter: 12 mm) as negative electrode and high-loading self-standing positive electrode (diameter: 12mm). Zn||ZnI2 pouch cell was assembled by using thin Zn foil (thickness: 20 μm, 25 cm2) as negative electrode and ZnI2 self-standing positive electrode (25 cm2) and were cycled under a fixed external mechanical pressure applied using a commercial clamping fixture (Guangdong Canrd New Technology Co.). No additional surface treatment was applied to the current collectors prior to electrode fabrication. A commercial glass fiber membrane (Whatman GF/D, pore size: 0.7 μm, thickness: 420 μm) was used as the separator for all the cells.

Electrochemical analyses
Galvanostatic charge/discharge tests of Zn||Cu, Zn||Zn, Zn||ZnI2, Zn||V6O13 Zn||MnO2 coin cells and Zn||ZnI2 pouch cell were performed using the Landt battery test system (Wuhan LAND Electronic Co.) and NEWARE battery test system (Shenzhen Neware Technology Co.). The Zn plating/stripping CE was measured in Zn||Cu cells by the Aurbach’s method and cycle method38,39. The processes of Aurbach’s method were as follows: First, the plating was deposited, cycled, and formed at 5 mA cm-2 and 10 mAh cm-2; then, the former plating was cycled again at 5 mA cm-2 and 6 mAh cm-2. Finally, the remaining Zn was stripped at 5 mA cm-2 until the cutoff voltage of 0.5 V was reached. Electrochemical measurements were performed on a Gamry workstation. Chronoamperometry measurements of Zn||Zn cells were conducted by holding cells at 0.07 V for 0.005 s. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were carried out in a potentiostatic mode with an AC perturbation amplitude of 10 mV over the frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.01 Hz, using 10 data points per decade. Prior to EIS measurements, the cells were rested at open-circuit voltage (OCV) for 2 h to ensure a quasi-stationary state. During data analysis, obvious outlier points were excluded from the fitting process. The cyclic voltammetry curves of Zn||Zn cells were tested at a scan rate of (2, 6, 10, 14 mV s-1), and the EDLC was calculated using Cc = i v-1, where Cc is the capacitance, i is the electric double layer current, v is the scan rate. The capacitance can be obtained from the slope of the i versus v. Here, i was defined as half the difference between current during the forward and reverse scans at 0 V, that is (i0v+ - i0v-)/244.

The mathematical expressions for classical nucleation models are provided below:
3DI: I/Im = (1.9542/tm) [1-exp(-1.2564t/tm)]^0.5 (1)
3DP: I/Im = (1.2254/tm) [1-exp(-2.3367t/tm)]^0.5 (2)
2DI: I/Im = exp{-(t/tm)} [1-exp(t/tm)] (3)
2DP: I/Im = (t/tm) exp{-(t/tm)} (4)

Characterizations
In situ eQCM was measured through the eQCM system (15M and Interface 1010E, Gamry) with Au-sputtered 5 MHz quartz substrates (diameter: 14 mm) to monitor the resonance frequency changes of the electrodes. The mass change of the QCM electrode (Δm) was determined from the resonance frequency shift (Δf) using the Sauerbrey equation. In the eQCM tests, 2 m ZnSO4 served as the BE, and the quartz crystal resonator functioned as the working electrode. Platinum wire and Ag/AgCl electrodes were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The cyclic voltammetry curves were recorded at a scan rate of 50 mV s-1, ranging from 0 V to 0.6 V. The QCM test was conducted in three steps: first, a frequency balance was established using a continuously flowing 2 m ZnSO4 electrolyte; second, the original solution was replaced with various additive electrolytes; and finally, the baseline electrolyte was reintroduced to monitor the frequency change and determine the formation of an adsorption layer. The electrolytes were delivered to the test chamber via a peristaltic pump at a flow rate of 1 mL min-1. In the Zn2+ hydration number test, porous carbon materials (Vulcan XC-72R, Cabot) and PVDF were mixed with NMP at a weight ratio of 9:1. The resulting mixture was uniformly coated onto quartz substrates and dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C. The coated quartz crystal resonator served as the working electrode, while platinum wire and Ag/AgCl electrodes functioned as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. CV tests were then performed starting from the open-circuit voltage in the negative direction at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1 ranging from 0 V to -0.5 V. During cyclic voltammetry, the charge stored or released on the electrode surface can be determined by integrating the current over time (the CV curve). The eQCM data were presented as the relationship between the electrode mass change (Δm) and the charge passed (ΔQ) during the negative polarization process45 (red and blue lines in Figures 3d,e).

To establish the theoretical reference for interpreting the eQCM results, the mass-charge responses of bare Zn2+ and fully hydrated Zn2+·6H2O were calculated according to Faraday’s law (dot and dashed lines in Figures 3d,e). These curves provide the expected Δm-ΔQ slopes for ions carrying either no hydration water or a full primary hydration shell. By comparing these theoretical slopes with the experimental Δm-ΔQ relations, the apparent molecular weight (Mw') of the interfacial species can be extracted using equation (5) 46. A deviation of the experimental slope toward higher apparent molecular weight than either theoretical limit suggests that the interfacial Zn species carry additional coordinated components beyond water.

MW' = (nF∙Δm)/Q (5)

Where n is the valence state of Zn2+, F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1), Q is the charge amount transferred through the electrode at presumptive 100% coulomb efficiency.

In situ FTIR spectra were acquired using a battery test system (Shenzhen Neware Technology Co.) coupled with a Thermo Fisher Scientific Nicolet iS20 spectrometer. In situ differential electrochemical mass spectrometry was performed using a commercial mass spectrometer (QMS 200 Atmospheric Sampling System, Stanford Research Systems, Inc., USA) connected to a sealed EL-CELL. Prior to testing, the system was purged with pure Ar at 1 mL min-1 for 12 hours; subsequently, the evolved gas was analyzed during charging and discharging at 5 mA cm-2 and 5 mAh cm-2, respectively. The entire cell setup was maintained in a temperature-controlled environment at 25 ℃.

In situ SEIRAS measurements were carried out using a Si ATR prism coated with a chemically deposited Au nanofilm. The prism was pretreated by immersion in HCl:HNO3 solution (3:1 v/v, 30 min), polishing with 50 nm alumina slurry (10 min), ultrasonic cleaning, oxidation in H2SO4:H2O2 solution (3:1 v/v, 20 min), and etching in 40 wt% NH4F (1 min). For Au deposition, 15 mL of Au plating solution was preheated to 55 °C, mixed with 3 mL of 2% HF, and the treated prism was immersed for 20 min, then rinsed thoroughly with deionized water. The SEIRAS cell employed the Au-coated Si prism as the working electrode and Zn foil as the counter electrode, and spectra were collected in situ during electrochemical cycling.

The interfacial electrochemical behavior of the Zn negative electrode was probed using scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM, CHI920D). In the SECM experiment, a Cu foil with deposited Zn served as the substrate electrode, while a Pt ultramicroelectrode (UME) with a 10 μm radius functioned as the working electrode. All SECM measurements were performed in a 2 m ZnSO4 aqueous solution containing 1 mM FcMeOH as the mediator. In SECM feedback imaging, the process involves scanning an ultramicroelectrode at a constant height above the substrate interface, variations in probe current reflect differences in surface topography and electron-transfer activity.

X-ray diffraction patterns (XRD) were recorded on Bruker D2, with Cu Kα radiation. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were taken by Thermo Fisher Apero 2s. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) data were required using an A PHI-5702 instrument with Mg Kα X-ray source, with a standard binding energy of 284.8 eV for C 1s. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were taken by Talos F200X. XAFS measurements were performed on the RapidSXAFS in Anhui Absorption Spectroscopy Analysis Instrument Co, Ltd. The Athena and Artemis modules of the Demeter software package were used to process the extended XAFS (EXAFS) data according to the standard procedures47. Wavelet transform was also conducted to analyze EXAFS data48.

Machine learning selection
A machine learning approach was adopted for feature selection to identify the most predictive combination of features for our regression model, with Coulombic efficiency designated as the target value. Our dataset encompassed a variety of chemical properties, including dipole moment, dielectric constant, donor number, molecular weight, and others (Table S1). Ridge regression was selected as the base model owing to its effectiveness in mitigating overfitting through L2 regularization. Polynomial features of degree two were generated to capture potential non-linear relationships between features. An exhaustive search across all possible pairs of these features was performed to evaluate their predictive performance, utilizing Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) served as the evaluation metric for assessing the predictive accuracy of each feature pair.

Calculation methods
The constant-potential molecular dynamics simulations were executed using LAMMPS software49, complemented with the ELECTRODE package. Initial configurations for the electrode-electrolyte systems were generated utilizing PACKMOL50 and Moltemplate (http://www.moltemplate.org/). The characteristics of H2O were depicted using the SPC/E model. For the force-fields parameters of the Zn2+ and SO42-, a combination of previous publications51–53 and RESP2 charges54,55 was employed. Similarly, the OPLS force field combined with RESP2 charges was utilized for the additives. To address electronic polarization, an electronic continuum correction method was applied with scaled charges (0.75). The simulation protocol began with Langevin dynamics at 500 K for 1 ns to facilitate salt dissociation. Following this, an NVT ensemble run at 500 K for another 1 ns was conducted to further promote salt dissociation. Subsequently, the system underwent an NVT run at 298 K for 5 ns to reach equilibrium without the application of a constant potential. Finally, to simulate the EDL structure under an electric field, an NVT run with a constant potential of 2 V was carried out for 5 ns. The binding energies were determined utilizing the ORCA software package56. Geometry optimizations of clusters were conducted at B97-3c level. Single-point energy calculations were then executed at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level. To adequately address long-range dispersion interactions, Grimme's D3 dispersion correction was applied. Visualization of the EDL structures was accomplished using VESTA57 and VMD58.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports an affinitive additive strategy for aqueous Zn metal batteries (ZMBs) that leverages high donor number and dipole moment molecules to enable electric-field-induced interfacial enrichment. Through a combination of in situ spectroscopy (eQCM, ATR-FTIR), molecular dynamics simulations, and electrochemical testing, the authors demonstrate that such additives can dynamically modulate Zn²⁺ solvation and guide uniform Zn deposition, resulting in a Coulombic efficiency of 99.9% and stable full-cell cycling even at high areal capacities. The work presents a novel angle for electrolyte design that emphasizes interfacial field responsiveness—a dimension often neglected in previous studies. However, some specific points should be addressed before the manuscript can be accepted for publication.
Q1. Why was the dielectric constant not chosen as a descriptor, given that it directly reflects a molecule’s ability to resist or respond to external electric field strength?
Q2. Although Zn deposition is excluded during eQCM measurements to isolate ion distribution effects, the difference in charge between Na⁺ and Zn²⁺ results in distinct interfacial electric field distributions. Would it be more informative to examine interfacial mass changes within the non-deposition voltage window of Zn²⁺ itself?
Q3. This paper also focuses on interfacial structural changes induced by organic additives. Could the authors more clearly differentiate their interpretation of interfacial dynamic evolution from those previously reported, especially in relation to the cited work: “Deciphering multi-dimensional interfacial mechanisms via organic cosolvent engineering for sustainable zinc metal batteries”?
Q4. Should the dynamic interfacial behavior of the electrolyte also account for changes after SEI formation? Wouldn’t this also fall within the scope of “dynamic interfacial structure” as discussed?
Q5. In Figure 2c, the baseline signals of the two electrolytes in the DEMS measurements are inconsistent. Could the authors explain this discrepancy?
Q6. In Figure 2d, please indicate the thickness of the highlighted interfacial region (distance from the electrode surface). Additionally, it would be helpful to plot the MD results for the no-bias case alongside for a direct comparison of interfacial structure under different field conditions.
Q7. In Figure 2f, a diagonal separation line could help clarify the classification of additive types. However, since both SL and ACN are considered shielding additives, how should their placement and distinction be interpreted?
Q8. In Figure 1b, the affinitive additives show significantly different effectiveness. What other factors besides donor number and dipole moment may influence their performance?
Q9. In Figure 5, only one electrolyte from a Nature-sister journal is used for comparison. Please include additional state-of-the-art electrolyte systems for benchmarking and better contextualization of the current work.
Q10. The activation step shown in Figure 5c involves a large number of cycles. Could similar Coulombic efficiency (~99.9%) be achieved using the standard 10-cycle activation protocol?
Q11. The authors attribute deposition behavior to solvation structure effects, yet the bulk electrolyte composition remains unchanged. Would it be more accurate to describe this as an effect of interfacial rather than bulk solvation structure?
Q12. Throughout the manuscript, terms like “affinitive additives,” “ERAE,” and “charge-reinforced” are used somewhat interchangeably. Please standardize this terminology to avoid confusion for non-specialist readers.
Q13. The color schemes used in Figures S17 and S18 are different, but the captions for both state "varying from yellow in plating to purple in stripping," which may cause confusion.
Q14. In the Figure 3 c schematic illustrations, organic additives are consistently shown occupying the first solvation sheath of Zn²⁺, which may lead to the misconception that all additives fully displace water. Please consider revising or reducing the number of such diagrams to avoid overgeneralization.
Q15. The Figure 3d-f suggests that affinitive additives can effectively replace water molecules in the Zn²⁺ solvation shell and that their large molecular size limits their access to carbon pores. In such cases, are the remaining coordination sites of Zn²⁺ left unsolvated (“naked”)?
Q16. While the current in-situ FTIR setup provides valuable information, it lacks surface enhancement, which limits its ability to directly resolve interfacial structural changes. Would the authors consider employing surface-enhanced techniques to strengthen this aspect of the work?

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the author used affinitive additive with high donor number and dipole moment to modulate Zn2+ solvation and the structure of the electric double layer under operational electric fields and to promote the stability of anode in zinc-ion batteries.
Although the electric-field-induced interfacial enrichment facilitates uniform Zn deposition and long-term cycling life of batteries, this work still followed traditional electrolytes papers in zinc battery filed, illustrating additive with different donor number or dipole moment. The novelty or performance are not significant and satisfactory. In addition, the overall quality of this manuscript cannot meet the standards of this journal as well. ### Reviewer 4

The authors herein developed an electric‑field‑reinforced affinitive additive strategy for aqueous Zn metal batteries, leveraging high DN and μ to create an electrolyte that dynamically responds to applied fields. The use of descriptors and MD theory calculations to develop electrolyte additive strategies has scientific significance. The mechanism of double-layer and solvation, as well as the description of morphology and electrochemical performance, are complete and clear, but the electrochemical performance is not outstanding enough, and there is relatively little chemical analysis of the microstructure of the anode and cathode surface. I would suggest a major revision based on the following comments:
1. The author screened 12 additives, covering a wide range of DN and μ, with each additive introduced at a fixed concentration of 2 wt%. Why is the concentration 2 wt%? Do other concentrations also follow the general pattern of DN and μ?
2. According to this paper, affinity additives need to balance DN and μ, but "DMU and MF emerged as the promising candidates (Figure 1c)" mentions that using MF and DMU as candidates. Figure 1c tells MF seem to be not as good as DMSO. Why does the author take MF and DMU as the two promising candidates? In addition, MF was not used in the characterization of the double layer and solvation structure, while DMSO and DMU were used to evaluate adsorption and desorption. Why?
3. This work believes that ideal additives have high zinc ion binding affinity and strong electric field responsiveness, which can accumulate at the interface and actively recombine zinc ion solvation under on-site conditions. The author should provide HOMO and LOMO for the three categories of additives (affinity additives, shielding additives, and inert additives), as well as the binding energy between additive molecules and zinc ions, to verify the advantages of ideal additives with high zinc ion binding affinity and strong electric field responsiveness from the perspectives of molecular reactivity and binding energy.

What is the average coulombic efficiency of shielding and inert additives? General Comment: This manuscript reports an affinitive additive strategy for aqueous
Zn metal batteries (ZMBs) that leverages high donor number and dipole moment
molecules to enable electric-field-induced interfacial enrichment. Through a
combination of in situ spectroscopy (eQCM, ATR-FTIR), molecular dynamics
simulations, and electrochemical testing, the authors demonstrate that such additives
can dynamically modulate Zn²⁺ solvation and guide uniform Zn deposition, resulting in
a Coulombic efficiency of 99.9% and stable full-cell cycling even at high areal
capacities. The work presents a novel angle for electrolyte design that emphasizes
interfacial field responsiveness—a dimension often neglected in previous studies.
However, some specific points should be addressed before the manuscript can be
accepted for publication.
Response to Comment: We appreciate your positive assessment of our strategy and
the recognition that electric-field responsiveness provides a novel design dimension for
Zn metal batteries. In this revision we substantially expanded both electrochemical and
mechanistic evidence. Long-term Coulombic efficiency measurements were added for
all electrolytes, confirming that only electric-field-reinforced affinitive electrolytes
(ERAE) sustain both high efficiency and long lifetimes. We also re-measured eQCM
for all electrolytes in 2 m ZnSO and complemented these with Zn-coated QCM
4
experiments, directly probing adsorption and desorption dynamics at the Zn interface.
To strengthen the spectroscopic evidence, we supplemented in-situ ATR-FTIR with
surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAS), which resolves
potential-dependent vibrational shifts that were not visible before. Finally, we
incorporated machine-learning validation showing that donor number and dipole
moment are the most robust predictors of additive performance under lean loading.
Together, these additions establish both the generality and the mechanistic foundation
of our field-responsive additive strategy.
Comment 1-1: Why was the dielectric constant not chosen as a descriptor, given that
2
it directly reflects a molecule’s ability to resist or respond to external electric field
strength?
Response to Comment 1-1: Thank you for this insightful question. The dielectric
constant indeed reflects how a medium responds to an external electric field, largely
due to cooperative reorientation among solvent molecules. However, its applicability
in interfacial systems, such as the electrode-electrolyte double layer, is inherently
limited by its dependence on collective solvent behavior and environmental factors. For
instance, ε reflects the averaged reorientation of many solvent molecules, which may
not directly translate to the local electrostatic interactions occurring at the nanoscale
electrode interface. Recent studies have highlighted this discrepancy, showing that ε
can vary significantly under confined conditions, such as in double layers (doi:
10.1016/j.jcis.2023.04.169). In contrast, the dipole moment serves as an intrinsic
molecular descriptor that directly quantifies how individual additives interact with
applied electric fields. Given our objective to assess the responsiveness of additives at
highly localized electrode interfaces, μ provides a more suitable primary metric for
screening purposes. That said, ε and μ can correlate approximately (Figure R1) and ε
may still serve as a complementary parameter; combining μ with selected bulk or
aggregate properties can improve predictive power when screening additives for
practical electrolytes.

General Comment: In this work, the author used affinitive additive with high donor
number and dipole moment to modulate Zn2+ solvation and the structure of the electric
double layer under operational electric fields and to promote the stability of anode in
zinc-ion batteries.
Although the electric-field-induced interfacial enrichment facilitates uniform Zn
deposition and long-term cycling life of batteries, this work still followed traditional
electrolytes papers in zinc battery filed, illustrating additive with different donor
number or dipole moment. The novelty or performance are not significant and
satisfactory. In addition, the overall quality of this manuscript cannot meet the standards

Response to Comment: We appreciate the concerns raised regarding the novelty,
performance, and overall impact of our study. In response, we have undertaken a
comprehensive revision—expanding both the conceptual framework and the
experimental foundation—to more clearly articulate the paradigm shift our work
represents in electrolyte design for aqueous zinc metal batteries.
We fully acknowledge that many prior studies have explored additives based on donor
number (DN) or dipole moment (μ). However, the core novelty of this work lies not
merely in the use of such parameters, but in establishing a field-driven, dynamic
interfacial regulation principles that fundamentally rethink how electrolyte additives
function under operational conditions. Below, we outline the key advances that
distinguish our approach from conventional additive-based strategies.
(1) Conceptual advance: field-responsive, low-loading interfacial regulation.
Traditional electrolyte engineering typically relies on static strategies—e.g., high-
concentration salts or organic cosolvents—to suppress water activity. In contrast, our
work introduces electric-field-reinforced affinitive electrolyte (ERAE), which exploit
22
the in situ electric field as an active driving force to enable reversible, potential-
dependent interfacial enrichment of functional additives at ultra-low loadings (2
wt%). This represents a conceptual advance:
(1) Instead of relying on static adsorption, ERAEs enable on-demand, field-driven
adsorption and desorption.
(2) Interfacial control is decoupled from bulk composition, minimizing side effects
on ionic conductivity and cost.
(3) The process is inherently dynamic and responsive to operational conditions—
aligning with real-world battery cycling.
(2) Predictive, validated selection rule.
We introduce a dual-parameter descriptor (DN and μ) that captures the two
mechanistic requirements at lean loading: sufficient Zn2+ coordination to co-migrate to

Response to Comment 2-6: Thank you for this insightful question. After rechecking
the analysis, we identified the origin of this behavior: poor statistical sampling in the
field-free (zero-bias) condition, not an error in calculation. In the absence of an electric
field, the local Zn2+ density near the electrode is very low (Figure R4), resulting in a
small number of interfacial ion events. This leads to high relative uncertainty in the
computed coordination numbers for additives like DMF and DMSO, which are present
at only 2 wt% loading. In contrast, under an applied electric field, the Zn2+ ions are
driven toward the interface, significantly increasing their interfacial concentration and
the number of sampled events. This yields much more reliable statistics and reveals the
true trend: field-enhanced accumulation of affinitive additives (e.g., DMU) in the EDL
and their partial displacement of H O in the Zn2+ solvation shell.

General Comment: The reviewer acknowledges that the authors have put great efforts
in improving the work presented in the manuscript, and that most questions from the
reviewer have been responded. However, the overall novelty is still quite questionable.
The emphasized "new mechanism" or "advances" seem more like a contrived or
strained explanation. The story actually still talks about a normal electrolyte
engineering based on additives when looking into the electrochemical behaviours
evolution. The authors provide a significant account of more characterizations
including operando/in situ operations, but these still cannot be considered as direct
evidence and could be explained by normal ways.
Overall, this manuscript presents a good research work, but the reviewer still feels that
the quality and significance are below the expected of Nature Communications.
Response to Comment: We sincerely appreciate your continued engagement with our
manuscript and your recognition of the substantial revisions we have made. While we
understand your remaining concerns regarding novelty, we would like to respectfully
emphasize that this work goes beyond incremental electrolyte engineering. It presents
a mechanism-driven framework for interfacial molecular selection in aqueous
batteries, rooted in a clear scientific narrative, distinct from recent approaches in the
literature, and validated through a closed-loop computational-experimental pipeline.
We outline three key aspects below:
1. The scientific story: From an unresolved contradiction to a predictive
interfacial principle.
Our research did not begin with screening additives followed by post hoc mechanistic
rationalization. Instead, it originated from a fundamental hypothesis about polarity and
Zn2+ desolvation. As illustrated in Figure S7a-c, we initially expected a volcano-type
relationship between polarity of organic additives and cycling stability. High-polarity
additives strongly coordinate water molecules, remain solvated in the bulk, and fail to
accumulate at the interface. By contrast, low-polarity additives lack sufficient
3
interaction with Zn2+ and tend to self-aggregate, also losing interfacial access. However,
none of the conventional polarity descriptors (DN, μ, ε) captured this trend in our low-
concentration regime. Intriguingly, even the recently reported ET(30)-based volcano
correlation1, while successful in high-concentration systems, showed inconsistencies in
our data: several additives within the optimal ET(30) window performed poorly. This
discrepancy led us to a pivotal realization: at trace concentrations, bulk-phase
descriptors are insufficient because they ignore whether an additive can actually
enrich at the electrode under operating conditions. This motivated our central
question: What molecular traits enable a uniformly dispersed additive to actively
migrate to, and persist at, the interface during polarization?
Through systematic analysis of physicochemical parameters (Figure R1), we identified
that only two properties govern the sequential steps of interfacial delivery: (1) donor
number (DN) enables Zn2+-additive co-migration; (2) dipole moment (μ) drives field-
responsive adsorption at the charged interface. Only when DN and μ are considered
jointly does a robust performance boundary emerge, resolving prior contradictions and
offering a predictive, mechanism-based descriptor, rather than an empirical
correlation. Guided by this DN-μ framework, we designed a suite of interface-focused
experiments, including measurements of surface affinity, desolvation kinetics, and
field-induced solvation reorganization. All consistently corroborated the model’s
predictions. Critically, our conclusions arise not from fitting data to a specific additive,
but from a descriptor-first, mechanism-predicted, and experiment-verified
workflow.
parameters influence additive behavior.
2. Distinctiveness from recent advances: A dynamic, field-responsive interfacial
pathway
As summarized in Table R1, many recent strategies toward Zn anode stabilization have
employed high-concentration additives, artificial SEI layers, or bulk electrolyte
restructuring. In contrast, our approach operates efficiently at just 2 wt% additive
loading and relies on an operationally activated, concentration-efficient mechanism:
additives with high DN and μ are selectively enriched at the interface during cycling
through the synergistic effects of Zn2+ coordination and electric-field alignment. This
results in a field-responsive associative solvation structure that dynamically modulates
Zn2+ desolvation and deposition, without perturbing the bulk electrolyte composition.
Unlike static shielding or thermodynamically driven passivation strategies, our
mechanism in inherently dynamic and electrochemically gated. It offers a new
perspective on how molecular design can harness operando electrostatic forces or
interfacial control, a concept potentially generalizable to other multivalent or aqueous
battery chemistries.

3. Newly added high-throughput validation: Demonstrating generality and
practical utility
To directly address the need for broader validation and real-world applicability, we have
newly incorporated a high-throughput computational screening workflow (Figure
7). Since direct computation of DN is expensive, we used the binding energy with Zn2+
as a practical surrogate. Starting from ~569,000 organic molecules in PubChem, we
applied successive filters for stability, safety, cost, and critically, our dual-descriptor
criteria:
(1) Electrochemical stability: adiabatic ionization energies > 10.4 eV and adiabatic
ionization affinities < 6.4 eV.
(2) High dipole moment: > 5.0 D.
(3) Strong Zn2+ binding: 0.18 Hartree higher than the Zn2+-H O interaction.
reduced to ~30 molecules after considering price and availability. From these, two
inexpensive and commercially accessible additives (piracetam (PIR) and 1-(2-
Hydroxyethyl)-2-pyrrolidone (HEP)) were experimentally evaluated in Zn||Zn
symmetric cells. As shown in Figure 7b, both additives significantly extended cycling
stability: the ERAE(HEP) achieved a lifetime of 270 h at 60% DOD, while the
ERAE(PIR) had already surpassed 465 h under the same conditions without failure and
was still undergoing testing at the time of writing. This result directly demonstrates that
our descriptor predicts functional interfacial behavior, not just theoretical affinity. This
newly added end-to-end pipeline, from mechanistic insight to molecular design rule,
large-scale screening, and experimental realization, provides strong evidence that our
framework is not limited to a few hand-picked examples, but constitutes a scalable,
rational strategy for electrolyte design.
Concluding remark
Although our system employs electrolyte additives, the core advance lies in uncovering
a general physical principle governing molecular selection at electrified interfaces
under dilute conditions. The newly added high-throughput validation further
8
underscores the robustness and transferability of this principle. We believe this
conceptual shift—from empirical trial-and-error to field-aware, descriptor-guided
design—offers timely and broadly relevant insights for the energy materials community,
aligning well with Nature Communications’ mission to publish interdisciplinary work
of high scientific and technological impact.

this study serve as the crucial basis for the discussion. However, significant changes in

previous response (Previous response to comment 1-8), the parameter set was updated
using tabulated solvent properties compiled by Roland Stenutz (stenutz.eu/chem). In
addition, in our initial submission, the DN-μ values for TAA and TBA were

Comment 4-2: Regarding "Response to Comment 4-2": As shown in Table S1, DMSO
outperforms MF in both donor number and dipole moment. Meanwhile, Figure S5
(revised) indicates that the lifespan performance of MF and DMSO as additives is very
similar. Given this, what is the authors' rationale for classifying MF as a "promising
candidate" (in Figure 1c) with a higher ranking than DMSO? It seems unnecessary to
make such a clear distinction between MF and DMSO.
Response to Comment 4-2: Thank you for your careful observation. In our work, we
initially screened and evaluated twelve widely studied additives at low concentrations
11
to establish a dual-descriptor criterion based on DN and μ. This criterion was developed
to identify electric-field-reinforced affinitive additives that could enhance Zn2+
desolvation and deposition efficiency. To demonstrate the generality and practical
utility of this selection principle, we selected two potential candidates, MF and DMU,
that meet the ERAE descriptor requirements and have received limited attention in the
context of zinc metal batteries.
Our subsequent tests confirmed that both MF and DMU exhibited durable
electrochemical performance, consistent with the predictions made by the DN-μ
criterion. Specifically, DMU possesses simultaneously higher μ and DN within our
additive library, indicating its stronger potential for both Zn2+ co-migration and field-
responsive interfacial adsorption. MF, while slightly lower in the parameters compared
to DMSO, still satisfies the DN-μ selection criteria and demonstrated comparable cycle
life performance in our experiments (Figure S3).
The reason for classifying MF as a “promising candidate” (now revised to “potential
candidate”) is twofold:
(1) Satisfaction with selection criteria: MF meets the DN-μ threshold, making it a
viable candidate according to our established framework.
(2) Additional practical advantages: While MF and DMSO exhibit broadly comparable
electrochemical performance in our tests, DMSO has already been extensively
reported in prior Zn-electrolyte studies and was therefore included primarily as a
reference compound for validating the DN-μ screening criterion. In contrast, MF
emerged directly from our descriptor-guided selection and remains largely
unexplored in the context of Zn metal batteries. For this reason, we chose MF as a
“promising candidate” to exemplify the ability of the proposed DN-μ framework to
identify new and previously overlooked additives.
We acknowledge that the initial phrasing of “promising candidate” might have caused
some confusion. To address this, we have revised the manuscript to use “potential
candidate” instead, which more accurately reflects the intended meaning.
Moreover, we emphasize that our primary goal is to identify additives that satisfy the
across all metrics. The observed similarities in lifespan performance between MF and
DMSO support the robustness of our framework, showing that multiple candidates can
fulfill the necessary conditions for effective interface stabilization. In conclusion, the
classification of MF as a potential candidate is justified by its adherence to the DN-μ
criterion and its practical benefits. Our revised terminology aims to better convey the
nuances of our selection process.

Response to Comment 4-4: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comment. In our
previous revision, we quantified the mass variation during potential cycling in ZnSO
4
electrolytes containing different additives using a peak-to-peak (P2P) approach.
Specifically, for each additive, the mass change (Δm) was determined by calculating
the difference between the maximum and minimum values (Figure R2) within each of
five consecutive cycles, and the average P2P value was used as an indicator of electric-
field responsiveness. However, because the absolute mass change during each
15
voltametric cycle was extremely small, this P2P method was highly susceptible to
baseline drift and high-frequency noise. In several cases, the noise amplitude was
comparable to or even larger than the true voltage-induced adsorption/desorption
response, which caused artificial inflation of Δm or Δm . This susceptibility
max min
explains the discrepancy you noted, for example, that the mass variation in the EG-
containing electrolyte appeared larger than that in the TEP-containing electrolyte,
despite their actual electrochemical behaviors.
As correctly pointed out, the direct comparison of Δm alone does not capture the
potential-dependent nature of the adsorption/desorption process, and this metric cannot
quantitatively reflect the amount of additive adsorption. Our initial P2P treatment,
defined as the difference between maximum and minimum mass within each cycle, was
highly susceptible to baseline drift and high-frequency noise, which can exceed the true
voltage-driven mass variation and lead to misleading trends.
Our intention in these measurements was to elucidate the adsorption/desorption
behavior of additives under a periodically varying electric field. In this revision, we
recognized that the applied potential follows a triangular waveform, and that the
additive response is strongly synchronized with this periodic modulation. To more
rigorously quantify this relationship, we introduced two complementary descriptors:
1. Pearson correlation coefficient (r), which captures the overall linear correlation
between potential and mass variation, thereby translating qualitative graphical
trends into a quantitative measure of trend consistency.
2. Amplitude Ratio (AR), obtained by extracting the fundamental-frequency
amplitude of both potential and mass signals via Fourier analysis. AR represents the
magnitude of mass modulation per unit potential amplitude (ng V-1), providing a
robust measure of the true electric-field-driven adsorption/desorption strength
independent of noise.
Accordingly, Figure 2b has been comprehensively revised using the combined
Pearson-AR framework. Additives located in the ERAE region exhibit pronounced
negative Pearson coefficients together with large AR values, indicating strong and
16
coherent electric-field-driven adsorption/desorption behavior. The full mathematical
procedure, including Fourier decomposition and AR calculation, is provided in the
Supplementary Information.

Comment 4-5: Regarding "Response to Comment 4-3": The calculated values of
HOMO and LUMO show a significant deviation from the typical value range,
particularly for the LUMO values.
Response to Comment 4-5: Thank you for this insightful observation. The apparent
deviation in the previously reported HOMO/LUMO energies indeed arose from the
inclusion of the SMD implicit solvation model in our calculations. As you correctly
note, gas-phase orbital energies are not directly comparable to solvated values,
especially for the LUMO, which is particularly sensitive to solvent polarization effects.
To address this concern, we have now recomputed all frontier molecular orbitals in the
gas phase at the same level of theory. As shown in the revised Figure S1, the gas-phase
LUMO energies across the molecular series are indeed much more consistent with
typical literature ranges, and the relative energy differences between molecules are
modest, as expected. More importantly, to provide a physically meaningful and
quantitative assessment of redox stability beyond orbital energies, we have performed
additional calculations using the xTB method to evaluate the adiabatic ionization
energies (AIEs) and adiabatic electron affinities (AEAs) for all candidate molecules
(Figure S2). These thermodynamic descriptors are directly related to electrochemical
oxidation and reduction potentials. Notably, our results show that DMU exhibits a lower
AEA compared to water, indicating that it is thermodynamically more difficult to reduce
than water under electrochemical conditions. This implies an expanded cathodic
stability window for the ERAE. We have incorporated these AIE/AEA-based analyses
into our high-throughput screening protocol and updated the manuscript accordingly.
In parallel, we expanded our study by adding a new high-throughput screening
workflow to explore a broader chemical space of potential additives. Because direct
computation of donor numbers is prohibitively expensive for large-scale screening, the
workflow instead incorporates a set of physically meaningful and computationally
accessible descriptors. Specifically, we now evaluate each molecule using (1) xTB-
level AIE and AEA as indicators of intrinsic electrochemical stability, (2) dipole
moment to reflect field responsiveness, and (3) Zn2+ binding energy as a practical
surrogate for donor strength. Molecules are retained only if they simultaneously satisfy
all three criteria: high oxidative stability (AIE > 10.4 eV), low reducibility (AEA < 6.4
eV), sufficiently large dipole moment (> 5.0 D) and sufficiently strong Zn-binding
affinity (0.18 Hartree higher than Zn2+-H O interaction). This newly included workflow
2
is presented in Figure 7a. Two inexpensive and commercially accessible representative
additives (piracetam (PIR) and 1-(2-Hydroxyethyl)-2-pyrrolidone (HEP)) that passed
all criteria were further tested in symmetric Zn cells (Figure 7b), the ERAE(HEP)
achieved a lifetime of 270 h at 60% DOD, while the ERAE(PIR) had already surpassed
465 h under the same conditions without failure and was still undergoing testing at the
time of writing, demonstrating the practical relevance and predictive power of the
screening pipeline.
